summary.text: A combination is a selection of k things out of n things, with no thing taken twice.
A poker hand is a 5-combination from a 52-card deck: the five cards are all different and their order does not matter.
There are 2,598,960 such hands, so the chance of drawing one particular hand at random is 1 in 2,598,960.

facts.label: Ordered versus unordered
facts.value: Divide ordered picks by the orders that give the same group

facts.label: Subsets of a set
facts.value: A set of n items has 2ⁿ subsets

facts.label: Allowing repeats
facts.value: Called a k-multiset or k-combination with repetition

facts.label: Whole-number trick
facts.value: Multiply and divide in turn; no remainders ever appear

items.prompt: You are dealt five cards and then swap two of them around in your hand, keeping the same cards. Is it now a different poker hand?

options.label: Yes, the new order makes it a different hand from before
No, the order does not matter, so it is the same hand
Yes, but only if the swapped cards are of different suits
No, unless the cards had been dealt in another order first

items.explain: In a combination the cards are all different and their order does not matter, so the same five cards are one hand.

items.prompt: To count 3-person teams from a club, you first count every ordered line-up of 3 different people. Why must you divide that number to get the number of teams?

options.label: Because some line-ups would use the same person twice
Because every team has exactly three captains to remove
Because each team appears once for every order of its members
Because teams sharing a captain would be counted together

items.explain: The line-up count includes each group several times, once for each order of its members; dividing removes those repeats.

items.prompt: A friend wants one specific, exact five-card hand to be dealt at random from a 52-card deck. What are the chances?

options.label: 1 in 2,598,960, because that many different hands exist
1 in 52, because each card has one chance in the deck
1 in 260, because five cards are drawn all at once
1 in 25,989, because the order of dealing is ignored

items.explain: There are 2,598,960 possible hands, and the chance of drawing any one at random is 1 in that number.

items.prompt: A bowl holds an apple, an orange and a pear. You pick 2 pieces, but now you may take two of the same kind. What changes?

options.label: Nothing changes, since you still pick from the same three
Every choice is now counted twice, once for each order
Only the choices that include the apple become possible
Three new choices appear, such as taking two apples

items.explain: Allowing repeats adds three selections: two apples, two oranges or two pears.

items.prompt: Computing 52 ÷ 1 × 51 ÷ 2 × 50 ÷ 3 × 49 ÷ 4 × 48 ÷ 5 in exactly that order never leaves a fraction. Why?

options.label: The divisions are saved for the very end of the calculation
Every running result is itself a count of combinations
Dividing by small numbers such as 2 or 3 never leaves a remainder
Each of 51, 50 and 49 is a multiple of the next divisor

items.explain: At each division the intermediate result is itself a count of combinations, so it is a whole number and no remainder appears.

items.prompt: Line up all n people in some order and take the first k as the chosen group. Why do many different line-ups give the same group?

options.label: Shuffling the first k, or the remaining ones, leaves the group unchanged
Each person can appear in the first k places only once overall
Line-ups that begin with the same person are always identical
Swapping people between the chosen k and the rest keeps the group

items.explain: Reordering the chosen k among themselves, or the rest among themselves, gives the same group, which explains the division.
